title: Introduction to Right Triangle Trigonometry
subtitle: Lesson 03
description: SOH-CAH-TOA, special angles, and reciprocal ratios via right-triangle diagrams.

steps.label: Introduction to Right Triangle Ratios
steps.subtitle: Identifying the sides
steps.bodyHtml: In any right triangle, there will always be two acute angles. (Why?) We select one of these angles as a reference, \(\theta\). Then we can identify the side opposite this angle as the opposite side. The side across from the right angle is always called the hypotenuse. This leaves the remaining side, next to the referenced angle, as our adjacent side.

steps.label: Identifying Sides of a Right Triangle
steps.subtitle: Referenced angle \(\theta = 30°\) vs. \(\theta = 60°\)
steps.bodyHtml:
Using the triangles below, identify the hypotenuse, opposite, and adjacent sides relative to the referenced angle \(\theta\).

hyp opp adj

Referenced angle \(\theta = 30°\)

hyp opp adj

Referenced angle \(\theta = 60°\)

steps.label: Example 1
steps.subtitle: Evaluating ratios from a right triangle
steps.bodyHtml:
Using \(\theta\) as a reference, evaluate each requested ratio using the right triangle shown here.

\(\theta = 30°,\ \dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}} = \) \(\dfrac{1}{2}\)     \(\theta = 60°,\ \dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}} = \) \(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\)

\(\theta = 30°,\ \dfrac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}} = \) \(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\)     \(\theta = 60°,\ \dfrac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}} = \) \(\dfrac{1}{2}\)

\(\theta = 30°,\ \dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}} = \) \(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\)     \(\theta = 60°,\ \dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}} = \) \(\sqrt{3}\)

steps.label: Definitions: Sine, Cosine, and Tangent
steps.subtitle: Right-triangle based definitions
steps.bodyHtml:
Sine\(\sin(\theta) = \dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}\)
Cosine\(\cos(\theta) = \dfrac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}\)
Tangent\(\tan(\theta) = \dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}\)

Note: there are three other (reciprocal) ratios possible — we'll save these for later in this lesson.

We can use the acronym, SOH-CAH-TOA, to help us recall the above ratios.

steps.label: Example 2
steps.subtitle: Using SOH-CAH-TOA
steps.bodyHtml:
Using the right triangle trigonometric definitions above, evaluate each of the following.

\(\sin(30°) = \) \(\dfrac{1}{2}\)     \(\sin(60°) = \) \(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\)

\(\cos(30°) = \) \(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\)     \(\cos(60°) = \) \(\dfrac{1}{2}\)

\(\tan(30°) = \) \(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\)     \(\tan(60°) = \) \(\sqrt{3}\)

steps.label: Example 3
steps.subtitle: A 45° right triangle
steps.bodyHtml:
Using the right triangle trigonometric definitions, find the sine, cosine, and tangent values indicated below. Click Build: mark the equal \(45°\) angles, add the two legs, then find the hypotenuse with the Pythagorean theorem.

\(\sqrt{2}\)

\(\sin(45°) = \) \(\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\)     \(\cos(45°) = \) \(\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\)     \(\tan(45°) = \) \(1\)

steps.label: Example 4
steps.subtitle: Trigonometric function values for special angles
steps.bodyHtml:
All sine entries have the form \(\sqrt{n}/2\), \(n = 0,1,2,3,4\). Cosine reverses the sine values. Tangent uses the identity \(\tan\theta = \sin\theta / \cos\theta\).

\(0°\)\(30°\)\(45°\)\(60°\)\(90°\)
\(\sin\theta\) \(0\) \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) \(\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\) \(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\) \(1\)
\(\cos\theta\) \(1\) \(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\) \(\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\) \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) \(0\)
\(\tan\theta\) \(0\) \(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\) \(1\) \(\sqrt{3}\) undefined

steps.label: Example 5
steps.subtitle: Solving for a missing side and evaluating ratios
steps.bodyHtml:
Using the provided triangle, evaluate each of the following.

\(2\sqrt{6}\)

\(\sin(\alpha) = \) \(\dfrac{2\sqrt{6}}{7}\)     \(\cos(\alpha) = \) \(\dfrac{5}{7}\)     \(\tan(\beta) = \) \(\dfrac{5}{2\sqrt{6}}\)

steps.label: Example 7 (a)
steps.subtitle: Reciprocal ratios, using the Example 5 triangle
steps.bodyHtml: \(\csc(\alpha) = \) \(\dfrac{7}{2\sqrt{6}}\)     \(\sec(\alpha) = \) \(\dfrac{7}{5}\)     \(\cot(\beta) = \) \(\dfrac{2\sqrt{6}}{5}\)

steps.label: Example 6
steps.subtitle: Standard position in the coordinate plane
steps.bodyHtml:
Plot the coordinate \((5,3)\). With this coordinate and the origin as vertices, construct a right triangle with base along the positive \(x\)-axis. Let \(\theta\) be the positive (counterclockwise) acute angle from the positive \(x\)-axis to the side formed by the origin and the given coordinate.

\(\sqrt{34}\)

\(\sin\theta = \) \(\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{34}}\)     \(\tan\theta = \) \(\dfrac{3}{5}\)

The line through the origin and \((5,3)\) is \(y = \dfrac{3}{5}x\). Notice anything about the slope? The slope equals \(\tan\theta\)!

steps.label: Example 7 (b)
steps.subtitle: Reciprocal ratios in the coordinate plane
steps.bodyHtml:
Consider the right triangle in quadrant I from Example 6, with vertex \((5,3)\).

\(\csc\theta = \) \(\dfrac{\sqrt{34}}{3}\)     \(\cot\theta = \) \(\dfrac{5}{3}\)

Looking ahead: any angle formed this way — from the positive \(x\)-axis to a ray through the origin — is said to be in standard position. We'll fully develop this idea in an upcoming lesson.
